name: Postal Museum
intro: The Postal Museum, or Postamúzeum, occupies the Benczúr House at Benczúr utca 27 in Terézváros, a late nineteenth-century mansion that later became a cultural centre for postal workers. Its permanent exhibition follows Hungarian postal, telegraph and telephone history through vehicles, switchboards, a period post office and hands-on machines.
about: The Postamúzeum is Hungary’s postal museum, housed in the Benczúr-ház at Benczúr utca 27, in the sixth district. The museum describes itself as a specialist museum with a national collecting remit, and it has been based in this house since 2012.

The permanent exhibition, titled “Elsők között…” (“Among the first…”), fills five rooms on the second floor. It looks at innovations of the Hungarian Royal Post: motor tricycles used to empty letter boxes in Budapest, women working on the telegraph and telephone from 1872, the first Hungarian postcard of 1869 and the Lakihegy radio tower of 1933. Among the objects are a Hughes printing telegraph of 1867, a tricycle from 1900, a liaison car from 1906, a manual telephone exchange from 1929 and a 1930s post-office room with a working pneumatic tube.

Much of the display is meant to be handled: the museum lists manual switchboards, Morse and telex machines, a touchscreen games station, letter-bundle making and a demonstration of sealing a valuables sack. A temporary exhibition changes roughly every six months, and earlier shows are moved into the archive section of the museum’s website, which also offers an online 3D walkthrough.

The house stands in Terézváros, the district around Andrássy út, and the connection is historic: from 1972 until the move to Benczúr utca the museum was in the Saxlehner Palace on Andrássy út. It is a specialist stop that suits visitors, and families in particular, who enjoy working machines.
tips: Check the museum’s official page before you go for current visiting arrangements, ticket categories and guided tours; the site has an English version, but its pages are written first in Hungarian.
The hands-on stations, including a Morse key and manual switchboards, make this a good choice for families. The museum also lists museum-education programmes for school groups.
The online MúzeumDigitár, photo archive and virtual walkthrough on the official site are useful for deciding what to look for before you arrive.
Andrássy út is the natural walk from here, and the former Saxlehner Palace, the museum’s home from 1972, is on it. Ask staff about photography rules when you arrive.

history.intro: The museum’s collection is older than its home. The two stories, one of an institution, one of a house, meet only in 2012.

sections.heading: From a telegraph room to a national museum
paragraphs: According to the museum’s own history, collecting began in 1881 in a first-floor room of the main post office in Budapest, starting with spare telegraph equipment. In 1890 the minister Baross Gábor ordered the establishment of a combined post and telegraph museum, which the museum treats as its founding.

A post, telegraph and telephone hall at the Millennium Exhibition of 1896 was meant to become the basis of an independent museum, but the hall was later demolished. Part of the collection was shown at the Transport Museum from 1899 to 1945, while the rest stayed in postal storerooms. A reorganised Postamúzeum opened in 1955 in the Postal Directorate General building as a specialist museum with national scope, and in 1972 it moved to the Saxlehner Palace on Andrássy út.

sections.heading: The Egyedi Palace on Benczúr utca
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia says the house was built in the late nineteenth century, then at Nagy János utca 27, as a residence and office building for Egyedi Lajos, whose family wealth came from a spirits distillery in Újpest. It names the architect as Marmorek Oszkár and mentions stained-glass windows by Róth Miksa; the article gives no exact year of construction.

In 1930, according to the same article, the Hungarian Royal Postal Charity Fund bought the palace. The museum’s official page says instead that the building was completed in 1931 for the cultural life of postal workers. The sources therefore differ by a year, and the dates are best read as 1930–31.

sections.heading: The Benczúr House and the museum
paragraphs: After the early 1990s the house belonged to a postal and telecommunications cultural foundation. Hungarian Wikipedia reports that its founders decided to close it in 2009, that Magyar Posta became the sole owner in 2010, and that the Postamúzeum has received visitors on the second and third floors since 9 October 2012. The official page dates the opening of the permanent exhibition to the same day. The building is a listed monument.

name: Kolibri Theatre
intro: The Kolibri Színház, or Kolibri Children’s and Youth Theatre, stands on Jókai tér in Terézváros, close to Oktogon. Founded in 1992, it stages puppet, family and youth productions in Hungarian for audiences from infants to young adults, and it also plays in two smaller venues on Andrássy út.
about: The Kolibri Gyermek- és Ifjúsági Színház is a repertory company for audiences from infancy to young adulthood. A 2016 profile on the website of the international children’s theatre association ASSITEJ described it as the only professional children’s and youth theatre in Hungary with its own company, and its official site sorts the programme into infant, child and youth categories.

It works in three venues. The main house at Jókai tér 10 presents family and fairy-tale plays and youth theatre, Kolibri Fészek at Andrássy út 74 stages performances for children aged up to nine, and Kolibri Pince at Andrássy út 77 is devoted to youth theatre. The official programme for autumn 2026 includes Lúdas Matyi, Micimackó (Winnie-the-Pooh), Bors néni, A világ születése and a new staging of Jules Verne’s Around the World in 80 Days.

Performances are in Hungarian. The website has an English section, but the official pages consulted do not say that any production is in English or without words, so check the programme and the stated age group for each show.

Jókai tér is known as the square of Hungarian literature. It was renovated in 2022, and short quotations from József Attila, Pilinszky János, Ady Endre and Kassák Lajos are displayed in the park. Across the way, on Liszt Ferenc tér, stand the Menza restaurant and the Írók Boltja bookshop, so the theatre sits among cafés and bookshops.
tips: Check the official programme for the performance, the age recommendation and the venue: the three stages are at different addresses, two of them on Andrássy út.
Most shows are in Hungarian. If you are visiting with children who do not speak it, look for puppet or music-led productions and ask the theatre before booking.
Tickets are sold online through the system linked from the official page. Leave time to walk through Jókai tér and its literary quotations before or after a show.
Liszt Ferenc tér is across the square, and Oktogon and Andrássy út are a short walk away. Keep phones silent during the performance and follow the staff’s guidance on photography.

history.intro: The theatre dates from 1992, but its house had a stage life long before. The building history below follows Hungarian Wikipedia, the only source found for it, so treat details as reported there.

sections.heading: A house with a theatrical past
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia says that Jókai tér 10 was built in 1912 as a residential building in the Secession style. A cinema called Edison occupied the ground floor, and from 1916 cabaret venues followed. In 1927 Rott Sándor opened the Komédia, which worked as the Komédia Orfeum from 1928 to 1944 and closed temporarily because of the war.

sections.heading: From post-war stage to puppet theatre
paragraphs: The article records that Medgyaszay Vilma reopened the house in 1945 as the Medgyaszay Színpad, later the Modern Színpad, and that it passed through several managers. In 1954 it became the chamber theatre of the Vidám Színpad. After a rebuilding in 1970 it served the Állami Bábszínház, the State Puppet Theatre, and from 1976 to 1992 it was that company’s chamber theatre.

sections.heading: Kolibri since 1992
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia says the Budapest Metropolitan Assembly founded the Kolibri Színház in 1992 in this building. The ASSITEJ profile credits composer and theatre director Novák János as its founder and executive and artistic director, and the Wikipedia article says he led it until 2025.

A new director, Zalán János, took over in 2025. Hungarian Wikipedia records that a large number of staff then left, and the theatre’s official site says new artistic, technical and management staff joined the company for the 2025/26 season.

sources.label: Kolibri Gyermek- és Ifjúsági Színház (official site)

name: Liberty Bridge
address: Between Fővám tér (Pest) and Gellért tér (Buda), Budapest IX / XI
intro: Liberty Bridge, or Szabadság híd, carries road and tram traffic between Fővám tér on the Pest bank and Gellért tér at the foot of Gellért Hill. Built for the Millennium World Exhibition and opened in 1896 as the Franz Joseph Bridge, it was blown up in 1945, rebuilt, and is still crowned by bronze turul birds.
about: The Szabadság híd is a three-span cantilever lattice iron bridge, 333.6 metres long and 20.1 metres wide, with a longest span of 170.75 metres. English Wikipedia notes that, although it is a cantilever bridge, its outline imitates a chain bridge, a look that was thought more attractive at the time. Its Art Nouveau decoration includes mythological sculptures and the national coat of arms.

Look up at the tops of the four masts for the bronze turul birds, a falcon-like bird from Hungarian mythology. Hungarian Wikipedia describes them hovering with outstretched wings 46 metres above the zero water level. The bridge is best appreciated from the embankments on either side or from a river boat, where its whole iron structure is visible.

The Pest end is at Fővám tér, in Ferencváros, and the Buda end is at Gellért tér, at the southern foot of Gellért Hill. The 2007–2009 renovation included the decorative lighting installed in 2009, which gives the bridge a distinct look after dark.

Trams cross the bridge along with road traffic. Since the 2009 reopening it has also been closed to trams and cars at some weekends for community events, and the transport authority BKK has tested the structure with every tram type in service. Check BKK for current routes and closures before you plan a crossing on foot.
tips: Check BKK for the current tram routes and any works or event closures on the bridge; it has been shut for weekend events and for works, so a planned walk across may need a plan B.
Fővám tér on the Pest side is by the Great Market Hall, and the Buda side is by Gellért tér and the Gellért Thermal Bath, so a crossing links two sights easily.
For photographs, the embankments at either end and a boat on the river show the whole bridge; the turul birds are best seen with a longer lens.
Do not climb the structure. A 2024 closure followed someone climbing it, and Hungarian Wikipedia also mentions a fatal fall in 2021.

history.intro: The bridge was one of the new Danube crossings prepared for Hungary’s millennium celebrations, and it opened in 1896. Hungarian Wikipedia gives the fullest account of its building and rebuilding.

sections.heading: A bridge for the millennium
paragraphs: A law of 1893 ordered two new Danube bridges in Budapest, including the one at Fővám tér. An international design competition drew 89 entries, and the design of Feketeházy János won second prize and was largely built as drawn. Nagy Virgil designed the architecture of the gateways, and Czekelius Aurél and Szántó Albert led the construction, according to the plaques.

Work began in 1894 with pneumatic caisson foundations, and the bridge was finished in August 1896. Emperor Franz Joseph opened it on 4 October 1896 and hammered in the last silver rivet. It was named Ferenc József híd after him; Fővám téri híd and Vámház téri híd were among other names in use.

sections.heading: Destruction and rebuilding
paragraphs: On 16 January 1945 the retreating German army blew up the central section. Reconstruction began in spring 1946 to designs by Sávoly Pál, and the bridge reopened on 20 August 1946 with its present name, Szabadság híd. It was repainted grey because paint was short. English Wikipedia lists the rebuilding year as 1945, so sources differ; the more detailed Hungarian account is followed here.

sections.heading: Renovation and the bridge today
paragraphs: The bridge was shut to traffic from 21 August 2007 for about 15 months. Trams returned in December 2008, cyclists on 30 May 2009 and cars the next day. The BKK reports that the bridge was last renovated in 2008, and in April 2024 it ran night-time load tests with every tram type in service as part of planning for a future Újbuda–Újpest tram axis that would cross it.

sources.label: BKK: New tram on Szabadság híd, load tests (2024)

seo.title: Liberty Bridge (Szabadság híd), Budapest
seo.description: Liberty Bridge links Fővám tér and Gellért tér: the 1896 Franz Joseph Bridge, its turul birds, wartime destruction, rebuilding and 2007–2009 renovation.

name: Mikszáth Kálmán Square
intro: Mikszáth Kálmán tér is a small pedestrian square in the Palace Quarter of Józsefváros, named after the novelist Kálmán Mikszáth, who lived in the corner house at number 1. A statue of the writer by András Kocsis stands in one corner, and terraces make the square a popular place for eating and drinking outdoors.
about: Mikszáth Kálmán tér lies in the eighth district, in the Palace Quarter behind the Hungarian National Museum. Tall buildings surround it, and it meets three streets: Reviczky, Krúdy and Szentkirályi. We Love Budapest reports that cars were banned around the turn of the millennium, and in summer the square feels like one large garden.

The landmarks are modest. The statue of Mikszáth, made by András Kocsis, stands in a corner, and Hungarian Wikipedia dates it to 1961. A commemorative plaque to the writer is by Kallós Ede, and a relief plaque for János Irinyi, the inventor of the match, is by Horvay János. The house at number 1 is now the building of the humanities faculty of Pázmány Péter Catholic University.

Today the square is known mainly for its terraces. The district council describes it as one of Józsefváros’s most popular hospitality and pedestrian spaces, and in 2024, after a hotel opened at number 3, it redrew the division of the terrace areas among the venues. In the 1990s the square was a nightlife area, with venues such as Tilos az Á and the Darshan Udvar.

It fits well with a walk through the Palace Quarter, whose former aristocratic residences, atmospheric squares and nearby National Museum and Szabó Ervin Library give the district its character. The council has been extending pedestrian-friendly street improvements across the quarter, and local notices sometimes announce temporary closures around the square, so check jozsefvaros.hu if you are planning a visit.
tips: Terraces are the draw, so choose a spot on the square itself and expect the area to be busy in warm weather. Check venue pages for what is on offer rather than assuming.
Look for the Mikszáth statue in its corner and the plaques on the house fronts; the plaque for Irinyi marks the site of one of his workshops.
The Hungarian National Museum and the Szabó Ervin Library are close by, so the square works as a break between two cultural stops.
Residents live all around the square, so keep noise down in the evening. The district council’s website announces temporary works or event closures affecting the square.

history.intro: The square’s history is tied to two writers and to one corner house. Sources agree on the main outline but differ on the exact year of the second renaming.

sections.heading: From Reviczky tér to Mikszáth tér
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia says the square had no name in the nineteenth century. In 1900 it was named Reviczky tér, after the poet Gyula Reviczky, who had died the year before. It was renamed after Mikszáth after his death: the Wikipedia article says 1911, while We Love Budapest says the square was renamed when he died in 1910, so the sources differ by a year. Reviczky’s name passed to a neighbouring street. Mikszáth lived at number 1 in his last years.

sections.heading: The corner house at number 1
paragraphs: We Love Budapest says number 1 stands on the site of a one-storey factory where the chemist János Irinyi founded the country’s first match factory in 1839; the factory moved out in 1869 and the present house replaced it. The Sacré Coeur Sophianum girls’ school moved in in 1917 and stayed until 1948, and the house was remodelled in 1926. The Piarist gymnasium used the building from 1953 to 2011, and the university faculty has been there since.

sections.heading: Statues, nightlife and terraces
paragraphs: A statue of a reading girl by Ferenc Kovács was set up here in 1954 and moved in 1960 to Tomori köz in the thirteenth district. The Mikszáth statue made for the fiftieth anniversary of his death followed. The 1990s brought a nightlife scene, and later the terraces, whose layout the district council revised in 2024 and set into its public-space rules in February 2025.

name: Zsámbék Church Ruins
intro: The ruined Premonstratensian church at Zsámbék, in Pest County west of Budapest, is a three-aisled basilica in late Romanesque and early Gothic style, built around 1220. Part of its vault fell in the earthquake of 1763, and since then it has stood as a protected monument, its two towers and stone arches still showing the scale of the original.
about: The Zsámbék Romtemplom is the remains of a thirteenth-century Premonstratensian church and monastery. Hungarian Wikipedia describes a three-aisled basilica with three apses and two towers but no transept. The south-eastern tower keeps its original stone spire, while the north-western tower is much lower and has a sheet-metal roof.

Visitors can walk around the ruin, which was reported in October 2025 to be fenced off yet open to visitors, and see the stone collection, the Kőtár, housed in the former monastery ruins beside the church. Hungarian Wikipedia lists a barrel-vaulted hall, the former refectory, the cloister foundation and a cellar system among the surviving monastery remains. The town of Zsámbék manages the site as part of its cultural centre, library and museum collection.

The heritage register’s photo caption calls it one of the most romantic places in Hungary and notes that it often hosts weddings and outdoor events. News reports add that it is built of soft sandstone that keeps deteriorating, which is one reason people disagree about how to protect it.

Zsámbék lies in the Budakeszi district of Pest County, and Hungarian Wikipedia places it 35 kilometres west of Budapest, at the foot of Nyakas hill. The town also has a baroque castle of the Zichy family, so the ruin can be combined with a walk in the old centre. Plan the journey with the getting-around guide, since this is a day trip.
A redevelopment of the site is being planned and is debated. Check the town’s official website for the current state of access and works before you travel.
tips: Check the town of Zsámbék’s official website, and the ruin’s own page, for current access, any works on the site and event days before you set out; redevelopment plans have been under discussion since 2023.
The Kőtár stone collection beside the church is part of the site, so ask on arrival where it can be seen. Wear sturdy shoes, since the ground in and around a ruin is uneven.
The ruin is a protected monument and also used for events, so treat the walls and stones with care and do not climb on them.

The two towers of unequal height are the ruin’s most recognisable feature and are worth photographing from a distance. The town’s website lists other sights in Zsámbék that can be combined with the visit.

history.intro: The church combines royal patronage, Ottoman-era upheaval and a nineteenth-century decision to preserve a ruin as a ruin. Dates below come from the town’s website and Hungarian Wikipedia.

sections.heading: A knight’s foundation and the Premonstratensians
paragraphs: According to the town’s website, King Béla III granted Zsámbék to Aynard, a knight who had come in the queen’s retinue, and Aynard’s descendants built the basilica around 1220. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that it was certainly standing before 1235 and gives its dedication as St John the Baptist. A Premonstratensian community lived in the monastery beside it, and Béla IV confirmed the church’s donation charter on 6 June 1258.

Hungarian Wikipedia reports that King Matthias gave the monastery to the Pauline order in 1475. After Buda fell to the Ottomans in 1541 the monastery became a fortress, and the Zichy family acquired Zsámbék in 1689.

sections.heading: The earthquake of 1763
paragraphs: On 28 June 1763 an earthquake brought down the vault and side wall of the north aisle. The church was abandoned, local people carried off stones, and the villagers built a new church in the town centre.

sections.heading: Saving the ruin
paragraphs: In the 1870s the historians Rómer Flóris and Henszlmann Imre urged that the building be saved. In 1889 the minister Trefort Ágoston commissioned the architect Möller István, whose work between 1896 and 1900, according to Hungarian Wikipedia, secured only what was structurally necessary and left the ruin as a ruin. In 1934 Lux Kálmán uncovered the monastery walls on the north side. In 2023 the town launched a design competition for the site, and a news report of October 2025 says the planning has begun but no construction date is set.
